corrosive

/kuh-RO-siv/ — stress on second syllable; rhymes with motive · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something corrosive slowly eats away at or destroys whatever it touches, whether that is metal, tissue, or something more abstract like trust.

The corrosive acid ate a hole straight through the metal tray.

Example

A father and daughter stop speaking after a bitter disagreement about her choice of college. For months, the silence between them grows and hardens. When they finally talk again years later, they realize that the corrosive resentment had eaten away at their once-close bond, leaving only painful distance and regret in its wake.

Corrosive describes something that eats away—whether it's acid dissolving metal, or bitterness dissolving a relationship. The word is more precise than 'harmful' because it captures the image of slow, chemical eating-away, and it can apply to abstract things like trust and love.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

harmful: Harmful is the broadest damage word — anything that causes injury of any kind qualifies, from a bruise to a scandal. Corrosive names one specific way of doing harm: eating away slowly at whatever it touches, the way acid works on metal or bitterness on trust.

acidic: Acidic describes the sharp, sour chemical character of acids — lemon juice is acidic, and so is a sarcastic tone. Corrosive is about the damage done: an acidic thing bites once; a corrosive one keeps biting until it has eaten a hole through whatever it touches.

biting: A biting remark is sharp and hurts in the moment, like a quick nip. Corrosive harm works on a different clock — it eats away little by little over months or years, so the damage comes from slow accumulation rather than from any single sting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

constructive: helping to build or improve something

preserving: keeping something intact and undamaged

Where it sits · how much lasting damage it does — harsh → abrasive → destructive → corrosive

harsh vs. corrosive: Harsh is milder than corrosive; harsh is merely rough or severe, while corrosive slowly eats away at whatever it touches.

abrasive vs. corrosive: Abrasive is weaker than corrosive; abrasive only scratches or wears a surface, while corrosive chemically eats through it over sustained contact.

destructive vs. corrosive: Destructive and corrosive both do damage, but corrosive specifies slow, eating-away destruction, while destructive can be sudden and total.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — cor-

Prefix — cor-: together; thoroughly (intensive) (Latin)

Root — ros

Root — ros: to gnaw (from Latin rodere, 'to gnaw,' whose past form gives ros-)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Cor- ('thoroughly,' an intensive) + ros ('to gnaw,' from Latin rodere) + -ive ('tending to') — corrosive describes something that thoroughly gnaws or eats away at whatever it touches over time.

Use the root in a new word: rodent

Use the root in a new word: rodent: The hardware store stocks traps for every size of rodent that might move into a garage over the winter.

Word Choice

neutral to formal

Corrosive names a specific kind of harm: something that eats away gradually, wearing down whatever it touches. Use it for acid on metal or bitterness in relationships. For sudden destruction or general harm, simpler words like 'harmful' or 'destructive' are often better choices.
